study_identification.author_journal_year: Meijer et al., Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 2024
study_identification.title: Toward Understanding Autism Heterogeneity: Identifying Clinical Subgroups and Neuroanatomical Deviations

study_characteristics.study_objective: To investigate whether reduction in clinical heterogeneity would lead to a reduction in neuroanatomical heterogeneity (i.e., greater homogeneity) in autism by combining clustering of clinical features with normative modeling based on neuroanatomical measures (cortical thickness and subcortical volume). The study aimed to parse clinical and neuroanatomical heterogeneity in autism using data from ABIDE.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer v7.3.2; Destrieux parcellation (148 cortical regions); ASEG atlas for subcortical volumes (23 subcortical ROIs)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Visual inspection and Euler number threshold (excluded individuals with values smaller than -300); N autism=15, N NAI=7 excluded due to low image quality; N autism=4, N NAI=1 excluded due to corrupted preprocessing (e.g., cortical thickness values of zero). The Euler number is related to the number of holes in the reconstructed surface and represents its complexity. Exclusion threshold of -300 was in line with previous reports using ABIDE I and II (Bethlehem et al., 2020).

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Site was included as a covariate in the normative model. The dataset consisted of ABIDE I (17 sites) and ABIDE II (19 sites), with sites having same/highly similar imaging acquisition protocols merged across ABIDE I and II to increase sample sizes per site (i.e., KKI and ABIDEII-KKI; NYU and ABIDEII-NYU_1; SDSU and ABIDEII-SDSU; and UCLA_1 and ABIDEII-UCLA_1). Sites with less than 10 individuals per diagnostic group were excluded (N autism=69, N NAI=15). No explicit batch removal methods like ComBat were mentioned; site was directly modeled as a covariate in the normative model.

modeling_method.answer: Warped Bayesian Linear Regression (wBLR) with 3-knot B-spline and SinArcsinh likelihood warping

response_variable.answer: Cortical thickness (148 Destrieux regions); Subcortical volume (23 ASEG regions)

predictor_variables.answer: Age; Site; FIQ; Euler number; ICV (for subcortical volumes only)

predictor_effects.answer: All covariates appear to be modeled as fixed effects in the Bayesian Linear Regression framework. No explicit mention of random effects or hierarchical structure.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses some aspects of nuisance structure but not comprehensively. Site is included as a covariate, and the Euler number (quality metric) is included, which accounts for some variance and mean shift differences across sites and image quality. The warped likelihood approach (SinArcsinh warping) allows for modeling non-Gaussian error distributions which addresses some shape/distribution issues. However, there is no explicit discussion of whether site is modeled with random effects or hierarchical structure to account for within-site correlation or site-specific variance patterns. The model does estimate separate noise parameters for each ROI to accommodate regional differences in population variation. Age nonlinearity is addressed with B-splines (3-knot). No mention of modeling heteroscedasticity explicitly or correlation structures. Overall, basic nuisance handling is present but not fully comprehensive.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Here, we performed normative modelling using the PCNtoolkit (version 0.26) in Python (version 3.9.16). We used a 3-knot B-spline Bayesian Linear Regression (BLR) model with SinArcinh likelihood warping and Powell optimisation, allowing us to calculate error measures in a warped space and describe deviations under a Gaussian error distribution... Included covariates in the normative model were age, site, FIQ, and the Euler number and also intracranial volume for the subcortical volume based normative modeling... Because we estimate a separate noise parameter for each ROI, this should accommodate regional differences in population variation (for example, the estimated variance parameter will be higher in the regions where there is greater variation across individuals).

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The normative model was trained on 90% of NAI (non-autistic individuals) and tested on the remaining 10% of NAI plus all autistic individuals. The 10% NAI test set comes from the same ABIDE I and II datasets, making it non-independent in the sense that it's from the same data collection effort, though the specific individuals are held out from training. Model performance was evaluated on this test set using standard metrics (SMSE, EV, MSLL, Rho).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: The dataset was split into a training set consisting of 90% of NAI and a test set consisting of all autistic individuals and the remaining 10% of NAI. We also ensured that age, FIQ and site were evenly distributed across the training and test sets... To evaluate the model performance, we generated the standardised mean squared error (SMSE), explained variance (EV), mean standardised log loss (MSLL) and the Pearson correlation between true and predicted responses (Rho) based on the NAI from the test set, as seen in Figure S4.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: There is no validation on an independent dataset within the same domain. The validation was only performed on a held-out subset (10%) from the same ABIDE I and II datasets. No external or independent autism neuroimaging datasets were used for validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: The dataset was split into a training set consisting of 90% of NAI and a test set consisting of all autistic individuals and the remaining 10% of NAI.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study only used ABIDE I and II datasets and did not validate the normative model on any different domain datasets (e.g., different scanner types, different acquisition protocols, different cohorts from other studies).
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: We combined the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) repositories I (Di Martino et al., 2014) and II (Di Martino et al., 2017) for all the analyses conducted in the present study.

clinical_groups_n.answer: ASD:690 (total for normative modeling); Clustering analysis: high-RRB subgroup:119; low-RRB subgroup:380

clinical_groups_age.answer: ASD overall: mean 16.12±8.88 years (range 5.1-64); high-RRB subgroup: mean 17.24±10.25 (range 5.9-62); low-RRB subgroup: mean 17.72±9.31 (range 5.3-59)

clinical_groups_sex.answer: ASD overall: F 0 (0%), M 861 (100%) for total sample before analysis-specific exclusions. Primary analyses conducted in males only due to limited female sample size (N autism=130, N NAI=280).

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score; Extreme deviations defined as |Z| > 2.6 (p < 0.005); Positive deviation indicates thicker CT or higher subcortical volume; Negative deviation indicates thinner CT or lower subcortical volume; Spatial overlap maps quantified as percentage of individuals showing extreme deviations in each ROI

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Model-based clustering (Gaussian mixture models with BIC for optimal cluster selection; bootstrapping with 10,000 iterations for stability assessment using Jaccard Similarity Index); Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for differences in ADOS-G subscores between subgroups; clusterpval package with 10,000 draws to determine significant differences in means between clusters while avoiding Type I error inflation; Permutation-based group comparisons (10,000 permutations) to test for differences in spatial overlap maps between subgroups and entire autism group, with FDR correction (p_FDR < 0.05, one-tailed); SVM classification with five-fold cross-validation to assess biological separability; One-tailed binomial test of balanced accuracy relative to null-information rate.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Two clinical subgroups primarily differing in restrictive and repetitive behaviors (RRBs) were identified, showing increased neuroanatomical homogeneity compared to the entire autism group, with the high-RRB subgroup showing increased cerebellar volume deviations and the low-RRB subgroup showing decreased cortical thickness deviations in postcentral gyrus and fusiform cortex; however, substantial within-group heterogeneity remained.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Model-based clustering identified two stable clinical subgroups in autism that significantly differed in RRBs (W=42,752, p<.001) and communication scores (W=19,396, p=.02), with Subgroup 1 (high-RRB, N=119) showing significantly higher RRBs and Subgroup 2 (low-RRB, N=380) showing more communication difficulties. The high-RRB subgroup showed greater overlap (increased homogeneity) in positive deviations in bilateral cerebellum (left p_FDR=.009; right p_FDR=.009) and subcallosal cortex (p_FDR=.017), while the low-RRB subgroup showed greater overlap in left cerebellum (p_FDR=.017) for positive deviations. For negative deviations, only the low-RRB subgroup showed greater overlap in left postcentral gyrus (p_FDR=.006), bilateral occipital fusiform cortex (left p_FDR=.014; right p_FDR=.013), right occipital pole (p_FDR=.006), left amygdala (p_FDR=.006), and left hippocampus (p_FDR=.034) compared to the entire autism group. SVM classification between entire autism group and NAI showed balanced accuracy of 65% (not better than chance, p=.8), and classification did not improve after subgrouping (high-RRB: 66%, p=.99; low-RRB: 65%, p=1.0). Individual-level deviation scores were highly heterogeneous with some individuals primarily displaying positive deviations and others primarily displaying negative deviations. Individual-level deviation scores were not significantly associated with any ADOS-G symptom subscores.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Limited to males only in primary analyses due to scarce female availability (N autism=130, N NAI=280), though supplementary analyses including both sexes showed similar patterns. High-RRB subgroup showed lower stability (JI=0.78) compared to low-RRB subgroup (JI=0.92). Substantial within-group heterogeneity remained even after subgrouping, as evidenced by lack of improvement in classifier performance and pronounced between-subject heterogeneity in deviation patterns. ADOS-G subscores are broad categories that cannot differentiate between different lower- and higher-order subcomponents, which may have different brain circuit associations. Equifinality - different genetic, environmental, and neurobiological pathways can result in similar phenotypic expressions. Limited power prevented further neuroanatomical clustering within clinical subgroups. Dataset limitations prevented examination of cognitive functioning, language abilities, and co-occurring conditions (ADHD, anxiety, OCD).
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study demonstrates that clinical subgrouping based on symptom profiles can reduce neuroanatomical heterogeneity to some extent, with subgroups showing more consistent (homogeneous) neural signatures in specific regions. The high-RRB subgroup's cerebellar findings align with previous literature linking cerebellar neuroanatomy to RRBs in autism. The low-RRB subgroup's findings in postcentral gyrus, fusiform cortex, amygdala, and hippocampus align with literature on social cognition deficits. However, the approach still leaves substantial heterogeneity, suggesting multiple pathways to similar clinical phenotypes and the need for deeper phenotyping with item-level scores and potentially joint clustering of clinical and neuroanatomical features. Future research should aim for larger samples allowing sex-stratified analyses and incorporation of additional neuroanatomical clustering. Authors note that differential patterns of autistic symptoms can inform screening, diagnosis, and future research into etiology and developmental trajectories, with potential for finding therapeutic targets and individualized support, particularly for individuals with high RRBs who may require specific behavioral interventions.

general_notes.general_notes: This study represents an important methodological advance by combining data-driven clinical subgrouping with normative modeling to address heterogeneity in autism at both clinical and neurobiological levels. Key methodological strengths include: (1) accounting for demographic variables (age, site, FIQ, ADOS module) before clustering to avoid subgroups driven by demographics; (2) using model-based clustering which provides probabilistic cluster assignments and automatic optimal cluster selection via BIC; (3) rigorous quality control with both visual inspection and Euler number thresholding; (4) comprehensive stability assessment with bootstrapping and Jaccard Similarity Index; (5) careful statistical testing using clusterpval to avoid Type I error inflation in cluster comparisons. The normative modeling approach used warped Bayesian Linear Regression with B-splines for age nonlinearity and SinArcsinh warping for non-Gaussian errors, implemented in PCNtoolkit v0.26. The study used a 90/10 split for training/testing. Sites with similar protocols were merged to increase sample sizes. Primary limitation is restriction to males only, though supplementary analyses with both sexes showed similar patterns. The study identified two subgroups primarily distinguished by RRBs rather than overall severity across all domains, which differs from some previous clustering studies. The finding that subgroups did not show improved classification performance suggests that clinical homogeneity does not necessarily translate to clear biological separability, likely due to equifinality. The paper provides thorough supplementary analyses including different subgrouping approaches (median split comparisons), FDR-thresholded analyses, and mixed-sex analyses. Code is openly available on GitHub. The study contributes to understanding that while clinical subgrouping can reduce neuroanatomical heterogeneity in localized regions, it does not eliminate it, pointing to the need for multi-level approaches combining clinical, neuroanatomical, and potentially genetic/molecular clustering in future large-scale studies.
